claim: TF-Engram is train-free: the backbone stays frozen and the memory table is built offline from an external corpus, so no gradient ever flows into the memory table.
stance_target: The repo's premise that frozen Engram-style memory tables remove memory parameters from the training graph
scope_conditions: Qwen3-0.6B backbone, offline construction from external corpora
quoted_support: We present TF-Engram, a train-free Engram system that constructs phrase-specific semantic memory offline from external corpora, stores large memory tables across a GPU-DRAM-SSD hierarchy, and uses Early-Exit Guided Predictive Prefetching to hide external-memory latency during autoregressive decoding.

claim: A 100M-entry TF-Engram table with 1024-dimensional FP16 vectors occupies 215.86 GB of storage, scaling nearly linearly with table size.
stance_target: How much storage a large frozen Engram table requires
quoted_support: The storage cost scales nearly linearly with table size, reaching 215.86 GB for a 100M-entry table with 1024-dimensional FP16 vectors.

claim: Keeping a 10M-entry table GPU-resident inflates GPU memory to 24.03 GB, whereas an SSD-backed 100M-entry table uses only 3.06 GB of GPU memory and shifts storage to CPU DRAM and NVMe.
stance_target: Whether tiered offload lets a small-VRAM GPU host a much larger memory table
scope_conditions: RTX 5090 32 GB, 64 GB host RAM, 516 GB SSD
quoted_support: A GPU-resident 10M-entry table incurs a large GPU memory footprint, increasing GPU memory usage to 24.03 GB. In contrast, the SSD-backed 100M-entry table reduces GPU memory usage to 3.06 GB, while shifting the storage burden to CPU memory and SSD-backed access.

claim: SSD-backed lookup without prefetching costs about 8.7% of decode throughput (481.2 -> 439.2 tok/s), and prediction-guided prefetching recovers most of it (Top-64 460.3, Top-128 462.4 tok/s).
stance_target: Whether external-memory lookup latency can be hidden at inference
scope_conditions: Qwen3-0.6B on RTX 5090, SSD-backed 100M-entry table, early-exit layer 8
quoted_support: The SSD-backed configuration without prefetching reduces throughput from 481.2 tokens/s to 439.2 tokens/s. With prediction-guided prefetching, throughput is gradually recovered. Prefetching with Top-64 improves throughput to 460.3 tokens/s, and Top-128 further improves it to 462.4 tokens/s.

claim: Decode latency overhead from external-memory lookup is small in absolute terms: 2.08 ms/token baseline rising to 2.16 ms/token with a GPU-resident 10M-entry table, and 2.175 ms/token at 100M entries with prefetching.
stance_target: The magnitude of lookup latency cost
quoted_support: The baseline Qwen3-0.6B model achieves 2.08 ms/token. A GPU-resident 10M-entry TF-Engram table increases the latency to 2.16 ms/token... Decode latency increases from 2.108 ms/token at 1M entries to 2.175 ms/token at 100M entries, while throughput decreases from 474.6 tokens/s to 459.8 tokens/s.

claim: Offline construction of a large TF-Engram table is cheap: 1.612 hours for n-gram extraction, 0.231 hours for embedding generation, and 0.157 hours for index construction.
stance_target: The one-time cost of building frozen memory offline
scope_conditions: Offline construction pipeline on the reported testbed
quoted_support: n-gram extraction accounts for 1.612 hours. Embedding generation and index construction take only 0.231 hours and 0.157 hours, respectively. This indicates that TF-Engram can be constructed with moderate offline cost, and that the main bottleneck is corpus-level n-gram processing rather than vector generation or index building.

claim: Train-free frozen memory still improves model quality: on Qwen3-0.6B the average downstream score rises from 57.6 to 59.4, beating both the frozen backbone and a parameter-matched LoRA baseline.
stance_target: Whether frozen memory can substitute for some fine-tuning gains
scope_conditions: Qwen3-0.6B, 100M-entry table, layer 8 early exit, Top-64 prefetch
quoted_support: On Qwen3-0.6B, TF-Engram improves the average downstream score from 57.6 to 59.4, outperforming both the frozen backbone and a parameter-matched LoRA baseline.

claim: Memory scale monotonically improves quality: average score rises from 58.2145 at 1M entries to 59.4092 at 100M entries.
stance_target: Whether larger frozen tables are worth their storage cost
scope_conditions: Qwen3-0.6B sensitivity sweep, table size 1M to 100M
quoted_support: As the memory scale increases, the average score improves consistently from 58.2145 to 59.4092.

claim: The best early-exit layer for predictive prefetching is layer 8: shallow exits give weaker prediction signals while deeper exits add compute and reduce throughput.
stance_target: How prefetch prediction quality trades against latency budget
quoted_support: The best result is obtained at Layer 8, achieving an average score of 59.4092... A shallow exit layer has lower latency but provides weaker predictive signals for prefetching. A deeper exit layer may produce more accurate predictions, but it introduces additional computation and reduces throughput.

claim: TF-Engram's evaluation hardware is a single consumer GPU (RTX 5090 32 GB) with 64 GB host RAM and a 516 GB SSD, so its results describe a single-GPU inference regime, not a multi-GPU training regime.
stance_target: Whether TF-Engram evidence transfers to a 5-GPU training box
scope_conditions: Intel i9-14900K, 24 cores/32 threads, RTX 5090 32 GB, 64 GB host, 516 GB SSD, 1 NUMA node
quoted_support: GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, GPU memory 32GB, Host memory 64GB, SSD storage 516GB, NUMA nodes 1.

claim: Hash-compressed GPU-resident Engram tables cause unrelated phrases to collide in shared slots, weakening phrase-level semantic fidelity - the motivation for TF-Engram's exact phrase-specific tables.
stance_target: The adequacy of hash-only Engram memory at small table sizes
quoted_support: existing GPU-resident designs often rely on hash-based compression, causing unrelated phrases to collide in shared slots and weakening phrase-level semantic fidelity.

claim: Naive external lookup can break decode latency because early transformer layers leave little computation to overlap with SSD or CPU-GPU transfer, which is why SSD-backed Engram requires predictive prefetching.
stance_target: Whether SSD-tier Engram memory is viable without a prefetch scheduler
scope_conditions: Autoregressive decoding with early-layer memory injection
quoted_support: host DRAM or NVMe SSD can greatly expand capacity and reduce hash collisions, but naive external lookup can break the latency budget... leaving little remaining computation to overlap with SSD or CPU-GPU transfer. Therefore, SSD-backed Engram memory requires an [predictive prefetch mechanism].
